Elevated PMD/DGD on a span can degrade coherent quality without affecting power or OCM OSNR. It would generally affect all channels on that span, but no DGD observation or corroborating affected service is provided.

An amplifier noise-figure rise could degrade receiver quality while amplifier input and output powers stay normal. However, downstream OCM OSNR showed no change and the effect should normally extend to every channel, making this unlikely.

A disconnected OMS input patch at S11 would suppress all channels into the booster and therefore cause amp1 input LOS and the broad service impact. It would normally also produce clear power loss at the booster input/output, which is not reported.

A sufficiently large sudden loss increase on the span could push every channel below detection and mimic a cut. The abrupt complete losses and critical LOS alarms favor a hard cut rather than a soft loss increase.

trace.assessment: The evidence localizes the cause to preamplifier oms.S04-S14.amp6. Its input power did not change while its output power changed immediately after a gain-out-of-range alarm, strongly indicating an internal gain-control degradation rather than an upstream fibre or source-power problem; the much later S15 OSNR excursion is on another OMS and is likely unrelated.

proposals.rationale: The local AMP_GAIN_OOR alarm followed by output power at -5.7, with unchanged amplifier input power, is the expected signature of gain falling below its set point. The absence of reported downstream service or receiver changes makes the severity uncertain but does not contradict a minor gain drop.

Ageing of the preamp pump could precede loss of gain regulation and produce a local minor alarm. However, no pump-current ageing observation was reported, and this mode normally holds gain rather than immediately reducing output.
A gain tilt could drive measured gain out of range and alter output while leaving input unchanged. It is less likely because there is no evidence of band-edge or channel-selective power changes.

A brief disturbance immediately before the preamp could transiently upset its gain control. The unchanged amp input power and the apparently persistent local output level argue strongly against this upstream explanation.

A partial or developing pump failure could cause local gain loss. A documented pump failure is normally hard and removes the output entirely, which is inconsistent with the minor alarm and nonzero output.

A shifted or narrowed passband can degrade one channel while leaving measured power and OCM OSNR unchanged, potentially forcing svc047 to protection. It is less likely because this is normally a sustained degradation rather than a brief transient and no receiver-quality symptom was reported.

Brief handling of a span or patch could cause a short excursion that was missed by sampled monitors and provoke the switch. The absence of any recorded power movement and the lack of contemporaneous maintenance make it weaker than an SOP-only transient.

trace.assessment: The outage was caused by a bidirectional fibre/cable break in the middle span between S10 and S21, represented by E7 in the S10→S21 direction and E15 in the reverse direction. The downstream amplifiers lose input while the upstream amplifiers remain normal, and OSC is lost on the corresponding span in both directions.

proposals.rationale: OSC loss on E7 and its reverse-direction counterpart E15, together with unchanged amp1 output and lost amp2 input in both directions, localizes a complete bilateral break to the middle cable span. The only minor counterpoint is that a sufficiently severe loss increase could produce similar telemetry.

A crushed cable, damaged splice, or severe bend in the middle span could remove both payload and OSC and create the same downstream power loss. Complete simultaneous loss in both fibres is more characteristic of a fibre cut than gradual or asymmetric added loss.

Handling or disturbance of the middle cable could affect both directions at the observed onset. However, this documented mode normally causes brief excursions, whereas the signals and services remain lost through t=1200 s.

trace.assessment: The cause is almost certainly a bidirectional fibre cut in the physical cable segment represented by E8 in the S04→S20 direction and E14 in the reverse direction. The paired OSC losses and amplifier power-loss boundaries localize the break to that segment and explain svc368 plus the wider simultaneous outage.

proposals.rationale: OSC is lost on E8 and on its reverse-direction counterpart E14, while S04→S20 amplifiers through amp2 and S20→S04 amp0 saw no change; downstream amplifiers lost input and output power exactly as expected from a cut in this physical segment. A very large non-cut loss could look similar, but the abrupt, complete, persistent, bidirectional loss strongly favors a cable cut.

A severe crush, bend, or damaged splice in E8 could suppress both payload and OSC and produce the observed downstream loss boundary. It is less likely because the loss is abrupt and complete in both directional fibres, which is more characteristic of a cut.

A hard ROADM degree failure at S07 could block all channels entering the S07→S16 line and produce the same downstream losses. It is less likely because the documented WSS fault concerns an arriving input port, whereas the evidence localizes the loss at the outgoing OMS feed.

A switch-fabric failure on the working ODU path could force protection without changing optical measurements. It should normally interrupt every ODU through that switch, whereas the neighbouring unprotected services remained healthy.

A channel-specific filter penalty could impair a working lightpath without a power change. However, receiver OSNR and pre-FEC BER showed no change at the relevant line interfaces, and simultaneous impact in both service directions is unlikely.

Added loss in the span immediately before amp4 could explain amp4's low input and the downstream channel-power reduction. It does not explain amp3's locally measured low output or its AMP_GAIN_OOR alarm, so it is unlikely.

trace.assessment: The event is best explained by a bidirectional cable cut on the physical 87.4 km segment represented by S04→S20 span2 and S20→S04 span0. The paired OSC losses, downstream amplifier input LOS, simultaneous multi-channel OCH LOS, and service/protection impacts all begin at t=602.5 s.

proposals.rationale: E8 is the S04→S20 fibre corresponding physically to reverse-direction E14; both report OSC loss at the same instant, with downstream amplifier input LOS and widespread channel loss. A fibre cut normally severs both fibres in the cable, matching the bidirectional hard failure; the only minor uncertainty is that a very large common loss could look similar.

A crushed cable, damaged splice, or severe bend on this physical segment could produce sufficiently large loss to lose both signal and OSC. The abrupt complete bidirectional outage is more characteristic of a cut than a soft loss increase.
